title: A Decade In, zeroRISC Sees A Bright Future For Open Silicon
gist: zeroRISC CEO Dominic Rizzo, who led Google's OpenTitan effort, argues open-silicon roots of trust are gaining traction thanks to IP-reuse economics, RISC-V, and regulatory and post-quantum pressure. The May launch of the Pavona ecosystem under GlobalPlatform, with Qualcomm, Analog Devices and Meta, aims to give open secure hardware a neutral home, with long-term governance as the open problem.

themes.theme: OpenTitan and open-silicon roots of trust

insights.claim: Google's Titan silicon root of trust, detailed at Hot Chips 2018 in the wake of Spectre and Meltdown, led to the open-source OpenTitan project, which Dominic Rizzo says was the first truly credible, well-resourced, from-scratch open source silicon project.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: OpenTitan is the foundation on which open-silicon security products and standards are being built.
insights.quote: OpenTitan was really the first truly credible, well-resourced, do-it-right-from-scratch open source silicon project.
insights.locator: The way I sold OpenTitan inside Google

insights.claim: Rizzo sold OpenTitan inside Google on the basis that buying lots of heterogeneous cloud hardware made the company's security posture lumpy.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Fleet heterogeneity is a security driver for standardized root-of-trust silicon in hyperscale data centers.
insights.quote: it made their security posture a little lumpy
insights.locator: The way I sold OpenTitan inside Google

insights.claim: Caliptra, a root-of-trust architecture including OpenTitan elements, had its first release in 2025, developed through the CHIPS Alliance and Open Compute Project by vendors including Microsoft, Google, AMD and Nvidia for datacenter-level SoCs.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Major silicon vendors co-developing an open RoT signals industry convergence on open security building blocks in the datacenter.
insights.locator: In 2025 came the first release Caliptra

insights.claim: More companies and groups are entering open silicon, including lowRISC (launched 2014), SiFive (emerged from stealth two years later), and the CHERI alliance (founded 2024) whose members include Arm, Google, the UK NCSC and lowRISC.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: A widening ecosystem of vendors and standards bodies indicates growing commercial seriousness of open silicon.
insights.locator: Over the past few years, the industry has begun to see more companies

insights.claim: In May, zeroRISC, Qualcomm, Analog Devices, Meta and the Max Planck Institute for Security and Privacy launched Pavona under GlobalPlatform as a neutral ecosystem for open, secure hardware design, chaired by Rizzo and modeled on how the Yocto and Zephyr projects work for software.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
entities: Max Planck Institute for Security and Privacy
insights.so_what: Backing by large chip and platform companies gives open secure silicon a standards-body home and a path to commercial adoption.

insights.claim: Pavona includes a production-stage post-quantum cryptography stack supporting ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA and a composable platform for building hardware roots of trust and chip subsystems.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: An open production-grade PQC stack lowers entry barriers for vendors facing PQC mandates.
insights.locator: Pavona includes a production-stage post-quantum cryptography

insights.claim: zeroRISC's silicon trust stack includes a Pavona collaboration repository with version control and CI, post-quantum-ready silicon IP, and a provisioning service with an HSM-backed line-side server and a management service for OEM debugging and over-the-air updates.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: zeroRISC monetizes through tooling, IP and provisioning services around open-source silicon rather than the silicon itself.

insights.claim: In May zeroRISC open-sourced a cryptographic hardware and software stack for classical and post-quantum use, with a programmable asymmetric cryptography coprocessor and dedicated accelerators for AES and SHA2/3.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Open crypto hardware can be adopted by SoC designers without licensing fees.
insights.locator: In May, the company unveiled the open source release

themes.theme: Why open silicon is gaining ground

insights.claim: The case for open silicon mirrors open source software: removing licensing fees and royalties charged by commercial chip makers like Intel, AMD and Nvidia, reusing infrastructure, faster innovation, supply-chain transparency and more eyes to find defects.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Open silicon is a long-run cost and trust challenge to royalty-based proprietary IP models.
insights.locator: The arguments for open silicon essentially dovetail

insights.claim: Open silicon never gained early momentum because of inconsistent interfaces and standards and highly specialized engineering roles, plus far fewer silicon engineers than software engineers.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Talent scarcity and fragmentation remain structural constraints on how fast open silicon can scale.
insights.quote: There is not really that kind of movement within those roles.
insights.locator: It has a lot to do with inconsistent interfaces

insights.claim: Modular chip design with widespread third-party IP from vendors like Arm and Synopsys and foundries like TSMC has normalized IP reuse, so lowRISC argues it is a small step for silicon vendors to adopt open-source IP instead of commercial IP.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: The IP business model has created the structural opening for open-source IP to compete with commercial IP vendors.
insights.quote: It is only a small step for silicon vendors to start using open-source IP instead of that from commercial vendors.
insights.locator: All chip designs today are modular

insights.claim: RISC-V, an open instruction set architecture introduced in 2010 and widely adopted in embedded systems with a push into the datacenter, gave permission for open source implementations by raising the question of why not open source the implementation if the ISA is open.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: RISC-V maturation is a tailwind for open-source cores and a risk to proprietary ISA licensing.
insights.quote: RISC-V almost gave permission because RISC-V is an open source instruction set architecture
insights.locator: In addition, the open RISC-V architecture continues to mature

insights.claim: lowRISC's Ibex CPU, released in 2019, is now used in various SoC designs, and Nuvoton brought to market a discrete OpenTitan-based root-of-trust chip that Google plans to use in Chromebooks.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Open-source silicon blocks are already shipping in commercial products.

themes.theme: Post-quantum and regulation as demand drivers

insights.claim: Governments in the U.S. and Europe are setting aggressive post-quantum cryptography deadlines because quantum systems are expected to break protections like AES-256, enabling attackers to decrypt already-stolen data in a harvest-now-decrypt-later threat.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Mandated PQC migration creates a multi-year demand cycle for PQC-capable silicon, firmware and provisioning.
insights.locator: PQC is a key challenge for the industry

insights.claim: Google has put the quantum threat timeline as early as 2029, while others look at 2030 or later, and the migration to PQC with ML-DSA, ML-KEM and SPHINCS+ is a once-in-a-lifetime transition for companies.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: A 2029 to 2030 horizon sets the window by which PQC hardware must be deployed.
insights.locator: Google has placed that time as early as 2029

insights.claim: Post-quantum cryptography is harder to implement than classical cryptography because there is no single hard problem at the root; trade-offs, underlying problems and implementations vary across operations.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Implementation complexity raises the value of ready-made, verified PQC IP.
insights.locator: PQ cryptography, it's a bit more of a pain to implement

insights.claim: The EU's Cyber Resilience Act shifts liability for cyber incidents onto device makers, pushing them to scrutinize their supply chains and gain greater control over what they build.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Regulatory liability is a demand driver for auditable, open hardware roots of trust.
insights.locator: new regulations like the European Union's Cyber Resilience Act

insights.claim: Rizzo argues software attack capability has grown to match the large software attack surface, so a silicon root of trust that can reset the system to a known good state is required.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Hardware roots of trust are becoming baseline requirements rather than optional features.
insights.quote: You need to have a hardware root of trust below the software that you can reset back to a known good state or all hope is lost
insights.locator: You need to have a hardware root of trust below the software

insights.claim: Building open silicon technology is understood, but sustaining it long term, building a real ecosystem and ensuring benefits go beyond a single supporter through governance remain the key open challenges.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Governance and funding sustainability are the main risks to monitor for open silicon projects.
insights.quote: How do you build the real ecosystem around it?
insights.locator: That's one of the more interesting aspects of this whole thing
